description: Soy Pablo Arroyo, Ingeniero en Nanotecnología con interés en la educación, divulgación científica en temática espacial y la astrobiología. Miembro fundador del Club Espacial de Chiapas (CHEC) y miembro activo de semilleros de investigación internacional de astroquímica y astrobiología.
summary:
The Last Contact On Earth is a pixel-art survival game for browser and mobile, built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. After the Selene-7 crash-lands at the lunar south pole with no fuel and no link to Earth, the player must plan and fly their own return mission:

- ISRU fuel: mine ice from a shadowed crater and turn it into water, oxygen and hydrogen (inspired by LCROSS, MOXIE and PRIME-1).
- Rocket repair: six subsystems based on NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab disciplines.
- Communications: design a CubeSat relay within mass and size limits.
- Return: launch inside a return window.
- Survival: manage power, oxygen, temperature, the day/night cycle and mental health.

A robot assistant guides players, and an unlockable archive links milestones to real NASA missions.

By turning systems engineering into decisions with real consequences, it makes lunar mission trade-offs tangible and accessible to students and the public.
details:
What it does / how it works
The Last Contact On Earth is a 2D pixel-art survival game, playable in any browser on PC, tablet and phone. After the Selene-7 crash-lands at the lunar south pole, Commander Alex Rivera has no fuel, a broken rocket and no contact with Earth. Players must design and fly their own return mission, guided by seven main missions:

  • ISRU fuel chain: mine water ice in a permanently shadowed crater, melt it, split it with electrolysis, then liquefy the gases into LH2/LOX at the 6:1 mix ratio.
  • Rocket repair: fix six subsystems based on NASA Goddard Mission Design Lab disciplines (propulsion, power, thermal, communications, attitude control, structure).
  • Communications: design a CubeSat relay with mass and size limits, then launch inside a return window.
  • Survival: keep oxygen, health, hydration, temperature, fatigue and sanity in check. Hazards include solar flares, micrometeorite showers, eclipses, heat peaks and leaks.
  • Base building: solar panels and batteries, an ice drill, Auto-Miner Rovers, an algae bioreactor and a hydroponic farm with crops you water and harvest.
  • Day and night: some resources only appear by day and others only at night, and the rocket needs both.

Mini Robert, a robot companion, explains every system, tells the player what to do next and can be upgraded at the Robert Station. An unlockable NASA Archive connects milestones with real missions and astronauts. Three historic sites (LCROSS, VIPER and Surveyor/Apollo 12) add real history to the map.

Benefits and intended impact
The game turns abstract mission-design ideas into decisions with visible consequences: power budgets, life support, ISRU, subsystem trade-offs and launch windows. Students and the general public learn by doing and failing, not by reading. Each crafting recipe and historic site carries a short "NASA Ref" line, and an in-game sources page separates real data from fiction. Our goal is to spark curiosity about lunar exploration and systems engineering in young people who might never open a technical document.

Tools and technologies

  • Code: TypeScript, React 19, TanStack Start/Router, Vite and Tailwind CSS v4 for the interface; Phaser 3 (WebGL) for the game world; Zustand for state.
  • Testing: Vitest and Testing Library, with more than 220 automated tests on game logic.
  • Delivery: GitHub, Lovable for building and publishing, and GitHub Pages as a mirror.
  • Assets: all pixel art and sound are generated in code, with no external assets.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code helped with programming.
  • Hardware: none; the game runs on any device with a browser.

Creativity

  • A survival game whose win condition is a mission plan, not combat.
  • Real NASA concepts (ISRU, MOXIE, PRIME-1, CubeSats, Goddard's six disciplines) used as game mechanics.
  • A human story told through the commander's diary and family album.
  • An HD-2D style with dynamic lighting, a flashlight, sun shadows and living biomes.
  • A day/night design that makes players experience the lunar cycle instead of skipping it.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty vs. fun: real data is cited, simplified values are labeled, and fictional elements (aliens, the crew) are marked as fiction. Return-window timings are still provisional estimates.
  • Accessibility: touch controls, larger text on tablets and PCs, a mandatory but short tutorial and a full in-game guide.
  • Performance: a high/low effects setting, with automatic downgrade on slow devices.
  • Difficulty modes: Easy, Normal and Hard, plus a Realistic mode with no aliens for educational use.
